title: drive-positron: pick distinct debug ports and verify CDP is Chromium
description:
### Summary
Fixes an exploratory-test launch flake where Playwright failed to attach with `Invalid URL: undefined` ([failed run](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/actions/runs/39402584237/job/118561027077)).
- `launch.sh` picked its four debug ports one at a time, so the same port could come back twice; that run got the same port for the browser debugger and the main-process Node inspector
- All four ports are now bound at once, so they're always different
- The CDP ready check now requires a browser websocket URL, so a wrong responder fails the launch and the workflow's retry loop kicks in

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- N/A

#### Bug Fixes
- N/A

### QA Notes
Dev tooling only, no e2e tags. Exercised by the next `/explore` or nightly drive-positron run.

title: Add a setting to choose the order of languages in interpreter pickers
description:
Addresses #15999
Design: #16672

### Summary

Adds an `interpreters.languageOrder` setting so users can choose which languages come first in the interpreter pickers and on the Welcome page.

- Settings shows every installed language as a reorderable list: drag, Move Up/Down buttons, or Alt+Up/Down
- Start Session, Execute Code language prompt, and Welcome page language cards follow the saved order
- Languages not in the order come after, alphabetically (today's behavior)
- A saved language that isn't installed here (e.g. synced from another machine) shows as "(not installed)" instead of an error, only in the User or Workspace tab that saved it


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2cefef61-4f37-4259-ae28-7f4fd330d910



### Release Notes

#### New Features

- New `interpreters.languageOrder` setting to choose the order of languages in interpreter pickers and on the Welcome page (#15999)

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

Open Settings, search "Language Order", and reorder each way:

1. Drag a row by its handle
2. Move Up/Down buttons on the row
3. Select a row and press Alt+Up/Down
4. Edit `"interpreters.languageOrder"` directly in settings.json

After each, check the Start Session picker, the Execute Code language prompt, and the Welcome page.

With a not-installed language (e.g. `"julia"`) saved only in Workspace settings, reordering in the User tab should not add it to user settings.




In dev builds the list also shows JavaScript and Zed. They come from dev-only test extensions and don't ship in release builds.

title: Send console, notebook, and Quarto Fix/Explain through an error assistant service
description:
Part of #13603. Adds a service shared by the Console, Jupyter notebook, and Quarto notebook Fix/Explain UIs. No Claude Code implementation yet.

User-facing changes:

- The console's Fix and Explain tooltips and screen-reader labels name the assistant ("Ask Posit Assistant to fix").
- Console Explain tells the assistant not to edit files, as notebook and Quarto Explain already did.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- N/A

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

Needs Posit Assistant installed and signed in to a model. Turn on `positron.notebook.enabled` and `quarto.inlineOutput.enabled`.

#### Console

1. Run `1/0` in the Python Console.
2. Hover **Fix** under the error. Expect the tooltip "Ask Posit Assistant to fix"; hover **Explain** and expect "Ask Posit Assistant to explain".
3. Click **Explain**. Expect Posit Assistant to open with "Explain this console error. Do not make changes or edit any files; just explain the error." and the error attached, and to answer without editing anything.
4. Click **Fix**. Expect a chat with "Fix this console error." and the error attached.

#### Notebook

1. Open `errors.ipynb` in the Positron notebook editor and run the cell.
2. Click **Fix** on the error output. Expect a new Posit Assistant chat with "Fix this notebook cell error." and the error attached.
3. Open the dropdown beside **Fix** and choose the option that continues the current chat. Expect the request to land in the chat from step 2 rather than a new one.
4. Repeat with **Explain** and expect the same, with the "Do not make changes" sentence on the prompt.

#### Quarto

1. Open `errors.qmd` and run the `divide` chunk so its error shows inline.
2. Click **Fix**. Expect a prompt naming the python chunk at lines 6-8 of `errors.qmd`, with the code and error attached.
3. Click **Explain** and expect the matching explain prompt.

#### `ai.enabled` off

1. Set `ai.enabled` to `false`.
2. Expect Fix and Explain to disappear from the console error, the notebook output, and the Quarto inline output without a reload. Set it back to `true` and expect them to return.

title: drive-positron: fix ui.sh, editor.sh and code every helper shares from the nightly run
description:
### Summary

Nightly self-heal: 2 helpers fixed, ready to review.

**To do:** Review and merge this PR.

#### finder-choose-menu-in-modal-dialog: fixed

- **What broke:** `ui.sh choose` on the Settings editor's More Actions button failed with 'no menu opened' and left the menu open, though the menu had opened.
- **Why:** It looked for the new menu in a way that cannot see menus VS Code draws inside a shadow root, as this drop-down does.
- **In a real run:** the agent hit it again: 2026-10-19T23:09:47Z ui.sh -s=positron: FAILED choose button 'More Actions... (Shift+F9)' 'Reset Setting': no menu, popup or list opened after clicking button "More Actions... (Shift+F9)" / 2026-10-19T23:09:59Z ui.sh -s=positron: FAILED click button 'More Actions... (Shift+F9)': the click on button ...
- **Fix:** It now also looks inside shadow roots, so it finds that menu and chooses from it, and `ui.sh click` names it as a menu.
- **Checked:** failed 4 of 4 tries before the fix; check.ts and all of smoke pass with it.

<details><summary>Evidence</summary>

**Reason:** Helper bug in the shared lib.markOverlays and lib.opened (scripts/page-lib.ts). Both searched for overlays with document.querySelectorAll (old lines 455-456 and 469-471), which does not look inside shadow roots. The Settings editor's More Actions toolbar is upstream VS Code code (settingsTree.ts sets renderDropdownAsChildElement, so DropdownMenu passes domForShadowRoot and ContextMenuHandler draws the menu in an open shadow root under .monaco-dropdown > .shadow-root-host; file-origin.sh says upstream, with no Positron block there). On the instance the page had one shadow host, and no light-DOM .context-view or [role=menu] while the menu showed. Playwright locators look inside open shadow roots, which is why ui.sh read menu and the 'view' found the menu while lib.opened returned null and choose said 'no menu, popup or list opened'. Fix: both evaluates query through a small 'all' that also walks open shadow roots, for the seen/home/list marks, the fresh-overlay search and the inline-list search under home. page.locator('[data-dp-list]') and lib.listIn already look inside shadow roots, so the rest of choose works unchanged. Helpers reached: ui.sh choose (the finding) and ui.sh click's 'opened' text. Without the fix, clicking the same button gave the generic 'a dialog, menu or quick pick opened; ...'. With it, the text is 'a menu: read it with ui.sh read menu'. Nothing else calls these two functions. Valid input is unchanged: light-DOM overlays are found as before. The new smoke ...

**Tries:**
- finder, fail: choose exit 1 'no menu, popup or list opened'; its view shows button [expanded] + menu with Reset Setting; screenshot shows menu open; read menu lists it
- finder, fail: after closing and reopening the Settings dialog: same error, exit 1; read menu lists Reset Setting, Copy Setting ID, Copy Setting as JSON, Copy Setting as URL, Apply Setting to all Profiles
- finder, fail: without --in dialog (the run's form): same error, exit 1; menu open; click menuitem 'Reset Setting' --in menu then works
- fixer, fail: Finding's steps on a fresh instance: choose exits 1 with 'no menu, popup or list opened after clicking button "More Actions... (Shift+F9)"'. The first try showed only the tooltip; on the second the menu opened and ui.sh read menu listed Reset Setting, Copy Setting ID, etc. The DOM has a shadow host ...

**To reproduce:**

```sh
settings.sh --session heal-find set editor.fontSize 16 --user
palette-run.sh --session heal-find 'Preferences: Open Settings (UI)'
ui.sh --session heal-find type 'editor.fontSize' --in dialog
ui.sh --session heal-find choose button 'More Actions... (Shift+F9)' 'Reset Setting' --in dialog --nth 1
ui.sh --session heal-find read menu
```

**Commit:** c05cd3ac0a31bd0d6b1c68efa18d6cee134a7de9

</details>

#### finder-editor-modal-not-text-editor: fixed

- **What broke:** `editor.sh` claimed settings.json was not a text editor when it opened in a modal, or silently read the file behind the modal instead.
- **Why:** VS Code shows no cursor position in the status bar for a modal editor, and the helper read the cursor only from there.
- **In a real run:** the agent did it by hand: 2026-10-19T23:15:45Z editor.sh -s=positron: FAILED type --at 13:8 ', ': the active editor is not a text editor (no cursor position in the status bar) / 2026-10-19T23:15:48Z editor.sh -s=positron: FAILED suggest: the active editor is not a text editor (no cursor position in the status bar) / 2026-10-...
- **Fix:** Every editor.sh command now says a modal editor is in front, names its file, and points to the button that moves it to the main window.
- **Checked:** failed 3 of 3 tries before the fix; check.ts and all of smoke pass with it.

<details><summary>Evidence</summary>

**Reason:** Upstream cause: VS Code's EditorStatusContribution (src/vs/workbench/browser/parts/editor/editorStatus.ts, upstream, no Positron block) creates status bar items for the main and auxiliary editor parts only, never for the modal editor part, so no 'Ln, Col' item exists while settings.json is in a modal. lib.editor in page-lib.ts read the cursor only from that status item and the DOM of the FIRST '.editor-group-container.active' (the main part's), so (a) with nothing open behind the modal every editor.sh command failed with the false 'the active editor is not a text editor', and (b) worse, with analysis.py open behind the modal, `editor.sh cursor` reported ok for analysis.py while settings.json was in front and keys went to the modal (type --at then failed 'the quick open did not open'). The fix is in the shared lib.editor, so every editor.sh command (read, cursor, goto, type, key, delete, insert, save, run, suggest, hover, definition) and qmd.sh's one lib.editor call inherit it: when a visible modal editor part is in front it refuses, naming the file and pointing at its 'Open Modal Editor in Main Window' button via ui.sh. Making editor.sh work inside the modal would need a cursor reader that does not use the status bar (column from DOM geometry breaks on tabs and loses the selection count), so it fails loud instead, as the finding's expected allows. New selectors: css.editorGroup.modal ('.modal-editor-part') and names.editor.moveModalToMain. Valid input change: with a modal edi...

**Tries:**
- finder, fail: settings.json opened in the modal via Open Settings (JSON) from the Settings dialog; editor.sh cursor and type --at 1:2 both exit 1 'the active editor is not a text editor'; screenshot shows the text editor with its cursor at 1:1
- finder, fail: after closing the modal and running Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON): dialog is settings.json, status bar has no cursor item; type --at 13:8 and suggest both exit 1 with the same error
- fixer, fail: After palette-run 'Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)', ui.sh read dialog shows dialog '.../User/settings.json' with a code textbox; editor.sh cursor exits 1 'the active editor is not a text editor (no cursor position in the status bar)' with tab ''; status bar has no Ln/Col button. With analysi...

**To reproduce:**

```sh
palette-run.sh --session heal-find 'Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)'
ui.sh --session heal-find read dialog
editor.sh --session heal-find cursor
editor.sh --session heal-find type --at 13:8 ' '
editor.sh --session heal-find suggest
```

**Commit:** 2e51707ecb124b67e8e0b6564e6bb7de853c2fde

</details>

title: Plan for pinning an interpreter per workspace (do not merge)
description:
**Do not merge.** This PR only exists so we can review the plan for #2659 with line comments and track changes to it.

## What's in this PR

- [`plans/2659-pinned-interpreter.md`](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/dhruvi/2659-pinned-interpreter-plan/plans/2659-pinned-interpreter.md): the decisions for #2659, as questions Q1 to Q14.
- [`plans/2659-implementation-plan.md`](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/dhruvi/2659-pinned-interpreter-plan/plans/2659-implementation-plan.md): how to build it, as 9 commits.
- [`plans/16376-discovery-cache-startup.md`](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/dhruvi/2659-pinned-interpreter-plan/plans/16376-discovery-cache-startup.md): the plan for #16376, which #2659 builds on.
- Reference docs for how startup works today: `plans/interpreter-startup-today.md` (the five startup steps the plans refer to) and `plans/extension-activation.md`. `plans/python-startup-policy-design.md` is Isabel's design for #15825.

## What the plan does

`positron.r.interpreters.default` and `python.defaultInterpreterPath` name a **pinned interpreter**. At every launch, core asks the language's extension for it and writes it over the workspace's affiliated runtime, so the pinned interpreter is what starts. When the workspace has no affiliated runtime for that language, the pinned interpreter reaches startup as the extension's recommendation instead (#15825).

Today these settings only apply to a workspace with no affiliated runtime. Once you pick an interpreter in a workspace, the setting is ignored there.

The pin decides which interpreter starts. `interpreters.startupBehavior` still decides when.

## How it meets the hard requirement

Review set one rule: core must not activate every language's extension before step 2 starts the affiliated runtime. #12645 made step 2 activate only the first language's extension, so an R console doesn't wait for the Python extension to load.

So core asks each extension for its pinned interpreter right after it activates that extension, never earlier. To ask, the plan adds one optional method to the runtime manager, `pinnedWorkspaceRuntime()`. Q14 has the details.

## How it relates to #16376

In #16376, R starts in a folder with no R files. R's interpreter search decides "start right away" from the open folder's files, and the discovery cache stores that answer and reuses it in every folder. The fix moves the decision into R's recommendation, which core asks for fresh in each folder. Q13 shows how that fits with a pinned R.

The #16376 fix also removes an unused `default` flag from R's cached records. Today that flag puts the pin into R's settings hash, so switching between projects with different pins makes R search for interpreters again. After the fix, it doesn't.

## Questions

1. **Is a new optional method on the runtime manager acceptable?** The plan adds `pinnedWorkspaceRuntime()`. We looked at two ways to avoid new API, and both have problems:
   - **A flag on `recommendedWorkspaceRuntime()`.** The first console would wait for the whole recommendation, which can wait for a full interpreter search. Also, the environment active in the shell Positron was launched from ranks above the pin, so the recommendation isn't always the pin.
   - **Swapping in the pin from `validateMetadata()`.** Core also calls `validateMetadata()` in the background to recheck cached interpreters. One folder's pin would then end up in the cache that every folder shares, which is the same kind of bug as #16376.

   The full comparison is in [the earlier working doc](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/5765199db335ebc748aef67a9c76c71e362c196c/plans/2659-pinned-check.md).

2. **Is it OK for a user-level setting to become a pin everywhere?**
   - Today a user-level `positron.r.interpreters.default` means "the R to use in new workspaces". It stops applying once you pick an R in a workspace.
   - With this plan, a value at any level, including the user level, pins every workspace at every launch. An R you pick in a project lasts only until the next launch.
   - So anyone who set it at the user level, and later picked a different R in some projects, would see those projects switch R after upgrading. `python.defaultInterpreterPath` changes the same way.
   - If that's too big a change, the fallback is: a user-level value stays a default for new workspaces, and only workspace, folder, or admin-enforced values pin.

## Decided since the last update

- **Q14:** core asks through the new method above, right after it activates the extension. It skips a language with no affiliated runtime. It also skips an interpreter you just picked in the New Folder flow, for that first launch only. From the next launch on, the pin applies.
- **Setting levels:** a pinned interpreter wins at every setting level, including the user level. Isabel and I agreed on this on 2026-10-15. Question 2 above checks that this is OK for R users.
- **Q13:** R's recommendation, not R's interpreter search, decides whether R starts right away, pinned or not. That's also the #16376 fix.
- **Startup time:** R's search for R files has no timeout, so R still starts in every folder that has R files. In folders with no affiliated runtime, the first console waits for that search. It took under a second in local tests, and it's slower on network drives.

## Still open

- Commits 7 to 9 in the implementation plan depend on Isabel's #15825 core changes and the #16376 R change, which aren't open as PRs yet. Commits 1 to 6 can be built now.
- Python's lookup of the pinned path can miss when it runs before Python's own interpreter search. When it misses, the old affiliated runtime starts for that launch. We need to measure how often that happens.

Comments on the decided questions are welcome too.

title: Let agents read widget and Quarto output in the Viewer
description:
Fixes #16377

### Summary

Follow-up to #16304. The `positronViewer.*` agent commands couldn't read two kinds of content that Positron shows in the Viewer:

- **Output drawn by notebook renderers**: console output sent to the Viewer, and a Quarto chunk's output opened there with the pop-out button (Plotly and so on).
- **HTML shown as a string, on Desktop**: Quarto's plain-HTML pop-out (`openHtmlString`). #16304 reported it as unreadable on Desktop.

Both are written with `setHtml` into the webview's `#active-frame`, which is same-origin with the webview's own `index.html` frame. So the bridge now reaches the content from that host frame:

- **Main process**: `IWebviewManagerService.getWebviewHostFrameId(webviewId)` finds the host frame by name; upstream names a webview's iframe after its ID. The frame must have a `vscode-webview://` URL and a parent that isn't one, so a frame inside the webview can't stand in for it. It searches every window, so a Viewer in an auxiliary window works.
- **Webview**: `getHostFrameId()` on `IWebview` / `IOverlayWebview`, inside the existing Positron blocks of the upstream files.
- **Bridge**: a self-contained `findViewerContentWindow(host)` goes to the `#preview-iframe` if there is one, or else `#active-frame` itself. Web builds call it from Positron's page, as `getAppWindow` did before. On Desktop it's serialized into the bridge script that runs in the host frame.
- **Desktop routing**: `ElectronPreviewOverlayWebview.callBridge` still uses the content frame for a loaded URI. A URI whose frame isn't known yet still fails with "hasn't loaded yet", rather than reading the host frame's empty page.
- **Content kinds**:
  - Renderer output is a new `output` kind.
  - HTML strings are `html` on both platforms.
  - `other` is now only previews that extensions make.
  - Output and HTML strings report no URL. Web builds used to report `about:srcdoc`.

The command descriptions and the positron-commands skill's `viewer.md` are updated to match.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- With Posit Assistant, AI agents can read and use output in the Viewer from a console session or a Quarto chunk, such as Plotly charts, and Quarto output opened in the Viewer on Desktop (#16377)

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:viewer @:quarto @:html @:apps @:assistant @:web @:win

**Tested on a Desktop dev build** (Windows), calling the commands through a probe extension:

- **Console HTML output that goes to the Viewer** (HTML with a `<script>` and a `<table>`): `positronViewer.read` gives `kind="output"`, and `positronViewer.click` on its button updates the page. The screenshot is correct.
- **A Quarto chunk's plain HTML, popped out**: read as `kind="html"` with no URL, and a click works.
- **A Quarto Plotly chunk, popped out**: the outline shows the chart and its four points.
- **An HTML file shown with `positronProxy.showHtmlPreview`**: read and fill still work, and the URL is reported.

**Not tested yet**: the web build on Workbench. Vitest covers the web path. A popped-out ipywidget renders blank for users too, so it reads as `(no content)`. That's an existing pop-out limit, not part of this change.

**To try it**: with Posit Assistant and `assistant.previewFeatures` on, run a Quarto chunk such as `plotly.express.scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6])` and pop out its output into the Viewer. Then ask the Assistant "What's in the Viewer?"

title: python (core): interpreter ranking refactor
description:
Part of #15825. Also addresses #16168 (envs one level deeper).

### Summary

First half of the Python interpreter ranking refactor. It adds the building blocks for one ranked list of Python interpreters. Apart from the discovery change below, nothing changes yet: nothing calls the ranking. The second half (recommendation, discoverer and filters) depends on a core runtime-startup PR and lands after it.

- **PET environment kind is kept.** `PythonEnvironment.nativeKind` carries PET's kind, so the ranking can tell pyenv virtualenvs from pyenv versions, and Homebrew/Xcode from other system Pythons.
- **Workspace scan** (`positron/workspaceScan.ts`): finds the root project env (`.venv` > `.conda` > `venv` > `.virtualenv` > `.pixi/envs/*`), envs one level deep, Python signal files, and `.python-version`.
  - It reads the root and each child folder once, with direct `readdir` calls.
  - It reads at most 1000 child folders and 32 at a time, and never uses `findFiles`.
- **The ranking** (`positron/interpreterRanking.ts`): the tier list, `tierOf`, `rankInterpreters`, `buildRankingContext` and `withDiscoveredFacts`.
  - `buildRankingContext` reads the launch shell's env through a new read-only `IActivatedEnvironmentLaunch.getActivatedEnvPrefix()`. The existing select call writes the selection; the new call never does.
  - `python.venvPath` and `python.venvFolders` are resolved by PET's own `getCustomVirtualEnvDirs`, now exported.
- **Nested envs are discovered.** Env folders one level below the workspace root (for example `app/.venv`) are passed to PET as workspace directories. The scan runs only when configuring for a refresh, not before every resolve.

Plan and decisions: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-25-python-startup-policy.md` and `docs/superpowers/specs/15825-interpreter-ranking-decisions.md` (local working docs). Design: #16572.

#### Behavior change: nested envs are now discovered

PET now finds `<folder>/<child>/.venv` (and `.conda`, `venv`, `.virtualenv`), which it did not before. Until the second half replaces today's selection logic, these envs go through the existing pickers:
- In a folder with no root env, a newly discovered `app/.venv` counts as a local env, so upstream's recommendation can make it the active interpreter for the language server and terminals.
- The current discoverer sort can put it first and, in a folder with Python files, mark it to start immediately.

This is the intended effect of #16168, but it is the one user-visible change in this PR.

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- Python environments one level below the workspace root (for example `app/.venv`) are now discovered (#16168)

#### Bug Fixes
- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:interpreter @:sessions @:win

Unit tests: `npm run test:unittests -- --grep "workspaceScan|interpreterRanking|Activated Env Launch|Native Python Finder - configuration"` from `extensions/positron-python`.

Manual:
1. Open a folder that has only `app/.venv` and `app/main.py`. The `app/.venv` interpreter appears in the interpreter picker.
2. Open a folder with a root `.venv`. Startup behaves as it does today.
3. Open `~` as the folder. Startup is not noticeably slower than on `main`.

title: Dev Containers: fall back to 127.0.0.1 when IPv6 is not available
description:
<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request.
If this is your first pull request you can find information about
contributing here:
  * https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

We recommend synchronizing your branch with the latest changes in the
main branch by either pulling or rebasing.
-->

The host-to-container operates via ::1, assuming that positron-server is listening.
The server binds to "localhost", which resolves to 127.0.0.1 if in some containers (e.g. if IPv6 is disabled).

In this case, the dev container starts and connects, but the client fails with:
> Failed to connect to the remote extension host server (Error: WebSocket close with status code 1006)

This PR replaces the assumption by trying ::1 first, but adds a fall-back to 127.0.0.1, in each of the `bash`, `nc` and `socat` variants.

An alternative would be starting the server with an explicit `--host`, but adding a fallback to 127.0.0.1 has a smaller footprint.

### Validation Steps

I can't not reproduce this bug. On both my devices I get this failure, but for those who do not get the error I suspect the following would reproduce it:

Open a folder with the following `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`: (disabling IPv6 inside the container so `localhost` resolves to `127.0.0.1`)
   
```json
{
  "image": "buildpack-deps:bookworm-curl",
  "runArgs": ["--sysctl", "net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=1"]
}
```

Run **Dev Containers: Rebuild and Reopen in Container**.

Before patch: the window fails with `WebSocket close with status code 1006`. With the container still running, the commands above show the server listening on `127.0.0.1` only.

After patch: Success :fire:

Much of the code (very small footprint) courtesy of Claude Opus 5.5.

title: Dev containers: fix positron-server download when using curl
description:
<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request.
If this is your first pull request you can find information about
contributing here:
  * https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

We recommend synchronizing your branch with the latest changes in the
main branch by either pulling or rebasing.
-->

After a devcontainer is started, if positron server is not present, it will automatically (attempt to) fetch a compatible version via `curl` or `wget`. There is a bug in the shell script when the container image supplies `curl` but not `wget`.

Specifically, the curl branch of the server install script piped curl's stdout into `tee | tar` while also passing `-w "%{http_code}"`. The status code is written to stdout, so is appended to the tarball and lost instead of being recorded in the `http_code` environment variable. The `http_code` variable, in the end, included the `gzip` error message along with the fallback `000`:
> gzip: stdin: decompression OK, trailing garbage ignored tar: Child returned status 2 tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now 000

This PR simply splits the problematic line into two steps: (1) download Positron server, and (2) extract the tarball. 

Fixes #12172

### Validation Steps

<!--
  Positron team members: e2e feature tags are auto-added based on your changed
  files, so tests run automatically when you open this pull request. Add tags
  here yourself to run more.

  - Instructions: https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/main/test/e2e/README.md#pull-requests-and-test-tags
  - Available tags: https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/main/test/e2e/infra/test-runner/test-tags.ts
-->

Use an image with `curl` but no `wget`, e.g. with the following `.devcontainer/Containerfile`:

```dockerfile
FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl ca-certificates \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
```

`.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`:
```json
{ "build": { "dockerfile": "Containerfile" } }
```

Run **Dev Containers: Rebuild and Reopen in 

**Before patch:**

We are greeted with a promising message
> Installing Positron server in container...

Followed by
> Failed to connect to container: Installation script failed: Command exited with code 1: Failed to download server from https://cdn.posit.co/positron/releases/reh/x86_64/positron-reh-linux-x64-2026.10.0-297.tar.gz (HTTP status:

**After patch:** Success!

title: Dev Containers: fix error at startup on Ubuntu due to shell issue
description:
<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request.
If this is your first pull request you can find information about
contributing here:
  * https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

We recommend synchronizing your branch with the latest changes in the
main branch by either pulling or rebasing.
-->


On Ubuntu, Positron devcontainers simply do not build. If you try, you are greeted with a popup:
> The terminal process "/bin/sh '/tmp/devcontainer-build-1791864524519.sh'" failed to launch (exit code: 1).

The easy fix is to just run `bash /tmp/devcontainer-build-1791864524519.sh`, which works.

A better solution is to fix the underlying cause: that Ubuntu points `/bin/sh` to `dash`, but the script uses `bash`-features. This PR replaces the one bit that `dash` actually rejects with a tiny workaround.

The current implementation uses `trap '…' ERR` (the `ERR` part is a bash extension) so that a failed build doesn't kill the terminal session, writing an error message for Positron, and exits 0. This fails on `dash` which does not have the `ERR` extension. This PR replaces it with an `EXIT` trap that checks `$?` and only fails when it is non-zero. Under `set -e` this is functionally the same.

Fixes #14943


### Validation Steps

<!--
  Positron team members: e2e feature tags are auto-added based on your changed
  files, so tests run automatically when you open this pull request. Add tags
  here yourself to run more.

  - Instructions: https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/main/test/e2e/README.md#pull-requests-and-test-tags
  - Available tags: https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/blob/main/test/e2e/infra/test-runner/test-tags.ts
-->

On a host where `/bin/sh` is dash (where `readlink -f /bin/sh` is `/usr/bin/dash`; e.g. Ubuntu and Debian):

Open a folder containing `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`:
```json
   { "image": "buildpack-deps:bookworm-curl" }
```

Then run **Dev Containers: Rebuild and Reopen in Container**.

Before patch:
> The terminal process "/bin/sh '/tmp/devcontainer-build-x.sh'" failed to launch (exit code: 1).

and `/bin/sh /tmp/devcontainer-last-build.sh` prints `trap: ERR: bad trap`.

After patch: Success!

title: Dev Containers: substitute variables in devcontainer.json
description:
Positron devcontainers ignore variable substitution in `devcontainer.json`. The existing implementation (`TerminalBuilder.buildAndCreate`) parses the json file with `jsonc.parse`, so variable definitions (e.g. `${localEnv:…}`, `${localWorkspaceFolder}`, et al) are interpreted literally. This affected `mounts`, `containerEnv`, `runArgs`, `build.args`, `image` and probably other legitimate usages. For example, `"source=${localEnv:HOME}/.gitconfig,target=/home/dev/.gitconfig,type=bind"` fails at container creation time, and in #12749 `${containerWorkspaceFolder}` expands to an empty string inside `postAttachCommand` which hits the same failure.

This PR switches a plain `jsonc.parse` call for the existing `substitute()` and `beforeContainerSubstitute()` helpers (untouches; defined in `src/spec/spec-common/variableSubstitution.ts`).

Fixes #12749.

title: 15714 packages pane filtering a scrolled list renders an empty pane
description:
## Summary

Addresses #15714.

If the Packages pane was scrolled down and you typed a search that matched only a few packages, the pane showed nothing even though there were matches.

The cause was in `PositronListInstance.setEntries`. It replaced the rows and set the new row count, but it never adjusted the vertical scroll offset. When the list shrank, the old offset pointed past the end of the shorter list, so the viewport drew no rows.

## Changes

- `setEntries` now clamps the vertical scroll offset to the new maximum scroll offset. This is the same check `DataGridInstance.setSize` makes and the Data Explorer instances make after filtering.
- `setEntries` now also moves the cursor back to the last selectable row when the list shrinks past it. Before this, the cursor could be left on a row that no longer existed, so `getCursorItem()` returned `undefined`, ArrowDown did nothing, and Shift+F10 / the ContextMenu key failed to open the row menu.
- Added a regression test to `positronList.vitest.tsx`. It scrolls a 200-row list to the bottom, puts the cursor on row 150, shrinks the list to 3 entries, and checks that both the scroll offset and the cursor are clamped.

The fix is in the shared `PositronList` component, so other lists built on it get the same behavior when their entries shrink.

## QA Notes

1. Open the Packages pane with a Python or R session that has enough packages to scroll.
2. Scroll to the bottom of the list.
3. Type a filter that matches a few packages near the top of the list (for example, the name of the first package).
4. The matching packages should be shown, not an empty pane.
5. Click a package near the bottom before filtering, then filter to a few results and press Shift+F10. The context menu should open for the last visible package.

title: Run the Databricks OAuth U2M sign-in in Positron so it works on Workbench
description:
Fixes #16409

On Posit Workbench, the Databricks OAuth User-to-Machine (U2M) mechanism could not complete. The `@databricks/sql` SDK opens the browser from the extension host and listens for the redirect on that host's loopback port. On Workbench the extension host runs on the server and the user's browser runs on their own machine, so neither step reaches the user.

The issue proposed mapping the loopback port through `vscode.env.asExternalUri`. That does not work: Databricks registers `http://localhost:8030` as the only redirect URI for its public `databricks-sql-connector` client and rejects any other redirect URI, including a Workbench port-proxy URL. The manual flow that Databricks documents for this case is the one used here: the browser ends on an unreachable `localhost:8030` page, and the user pastes that page's address back.

### Summary

Positron now runs the authorization-code flow itself instead of delegating it to the SDK:

- `databricksOAuth.ts` holds the flow's building blocks: endpoint discovery, the PKCE authorization request, callback parsing, token exchange and refresh, and a loopback listener. It imports nothing from `vscode`, so Vitest covers it.
- `databricksSignIn.ts` opens the browser with `vscode.env.openExternal`, listens on port 8030 when the port is free, and shows an input box titled **Sign in to Databricks**. The redirect completes the sign-in by whichever route arrives first: the listener (desktop Positron, or a remote whose port is forwarded) or the pasted address (Workbench). The input box validates the pasted address against the request's state.
- The driver signs in before it builds the connection and hands the session's token provider to the SDK through its `external-token` path. One sign-in serves the connection for its whole life, including reconnects, and the access token is refreshed ahead of expiry.

The redirect URI stays `http://localhost:8030`, so desktop behavior is unchanged apart from the browser now opening through `vscode.env.openExternal`. On Azure Databricks the sign-in now uses Databricks' native OAuth endpoints rather than Entra; the SDK supports this mode, but it was not tried against an Azure workspace.

The Snowflake `externalbrowser` mechanism has the same remote-host problem and is not changed here.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- N/A

#### Bug Fixes

- Databricks Data Connections can now sign in with OAuth User-to-Machine on Posit Workbench. Positron opens the user's browser and, when the redirect cannot reach Positron, accepts the redirect address pasted back (#16409).

### Validation Steps

@:connections @:workbench-databricks

Unit tests:

- `npx vitest run extensions/positron-data-driver-databricks/src/databricksOAuth.vitest.ts` covers discovery, the PKCE request, callback parsing, token exchange and refresh, session refresh, and the loopback listener.
- `npm run test-extension -- -l positron-data-driver-databricks` covers the mechanism-to-SDK option mapping.

End to end on Workbench:

- The new `test/e2e/tests/workbench/data-connections/databricks-oauth-u2m.test.ts` adds a U2M connection, signs in through **Continue with SSO** with the IDE service account (Okta password and TOTP), reads the `localhost:8030` redirect off the popup, pastes it into the **Sign in to Databricks** prompt, and expects the connection to list its catalogs. The Workbench workflow now passes `DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH` from the same 1Password item the Ubuntu lane reads, which the test needs. Passed three times locally against `npm run pwb -- --workbench=daily --positron=daily --credentials=databricks`.

Manually on Workbench:

1. Open the Data Connections pane and add a Databricks connection with the **OAuth User-to-Machine (U2M)** mechanism, a Server Hostname, and an HTTP Path.
2. Expand the connection. A browser tab opens on the workspace sign-in page, and Positron shows the **Sign in to Databricks** prompt.
3. Sign in. The tab ends on a `http://localhost:8030/?code=...` page that cannot be reached.
4. Copy that tab's address, paste it into the prompt, and press Enter. The connection lists the workspace's catalogs.

Manually on desktop: the same steps, except the sign-in completes on its own after step 3 and the prompt closes.

title: Implement `file.choose()` for R
description: In Positron, R's `file.choose()` asks you to type a file name in the console instead of opening a file picker. This PR adds a new `select_file` request to the UI comm so that the kernel can ask Positron to show a file dialog and return the chosen path. - If the file must already exist, Positron shows an Open dialog. Otherwise (`file.choose(new = TRUE)`), it shows a Save dialog so you can enter a new file name. - The dialog starts in the directory the kernel sends (the R working directory). - If you cancel, the request returns `null`, and R gives its usual "file choice cancelled" error. This PR also bumps the Ark submodule to pick up the companion Ark change. Related PR: posit-dev/ark#1442 (makes `file.choose()` send the new request) Fixes #16633. ### Release Notes #### New Features - N/A #### Bug Fixes - R's `file.choose()` now opens a file dialog instead of prompting for a file name in the console (#16633) ### Validation Steps @:ark @:console 1. Start an R session (macOS or Linux; Windows R uses its own native dialog). 2. Run `fname <- file.choose()`. A file dialog should open in the current working directory. Pick a file and check that `fname` is its full path. 3. Run `file.choose(new = TRUE)`. A save dialog should open, and you should be able to type a file name that doesn't exist yet. 4. Run `file.choose()` again and cancel the dialog. You should see the "file choice cancelled" error. 5. Repeat step 2 in Positron Web and check that the path is returned correctly.

title: Hand AI provider sign-in to Posit Assistant
description:
Posit Assistant takes over AI provider sign-in from Positron's authentication extension. This replaces #16102, re-cut onto current main.

Closes #16370.

### What moves to Assistant

- Sign-in for Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenAI-compatible, DeepSeek, Posit AI Pass, Foundry, Vertex, Snowflake, Databricks and custom providers.
- Positron's provider dialog is removed. **Configure Language Model Providers** in the Accounts menu runs Assistant's `posit-assistant.configureProviders`. If Assistant is turned off or not installed, it shows a message with a button to open Assistant's Extensions page.
- On first start, Positron copies stored API keys (including Snowflake and Databricks personal access tokens), custom provider keys and the Posit AI Pass session into Assistant's store, so people don't have to sign in again. Databricks OAuth sign-ins aren't copied, since Assistant doesn't support Databricks OAuth on Positron yet.

### What the authentication extension keeps

- The Bedrock sign-in (AWS credential chain).
- Snowflake and Databricks sign-in, but only while the bundled Assistant doesn't declare those providers. Once Assistant is bumped, Assistant owns them and the extension stops registering them.
- Workbench-managed Snowflake and Databricks credentials for the data connection drivers (the `managedCredentials` export).
- Moving old settings into providers.json, turning Posit AI Pass off by default on Workbench, and reporting provider status to **AI: Create Diagnostic Report**.

On Workbench, Foundry's managed sign-in now goes through Assistant, so the authentication extension's Workbench sign-in code is removed. The providers.json editing helpers that Positron's provider dialog used are removed too, since Assistant's provider screen does that now.

### Other changes

- Auth provider ids now match the provider catalog ids (`amazon-bedrock` becomes `bedrock`, `posit-ai` becomes `positai`, and so on). `product.json` grants Assistant access under the new ids.
- The `positron.ai` API drops provider registration and the other leftovers from Positron Assistant (`registerProvider`, `registerChatAgent`, `getCurrentProvider`, etc.). It adds `getProviderBaseUrl()` and `onDidChangeProviderEnablement`.
- Next Edit Suggestions reads the Posit AI Pass base URL from Positron's provider catalog through `positron.ai.getProviderBaseUrl()`, so it no longer depends on the authentication extension.
- Language model vendors the provider catalog doesn't know about (such as Copilot's bring-your-own-key vendors) count as turned off, so they can't become the default chat provider.
- The headless language model service reads custom provider credentials from Assistant's `custom-providers` sign-in.
- The Posit Assistant e2e tests sign in through Assistant's provider screen, and the Workbench, remote SSH, MCP, release-screenshot and eval runs use it too.

### Before this is ready

- posit-dev/assistant#2603 (Assistant takes over sign-in, including the Snowflake and Databricks auth providers) needs to merge and ship.
- Bump the bundled Assistant in `product.json` to the release that carries posit-dev/assistant#2603 and posit-dev/assistant#2600 (third-party terms notice, already merged).
- posit-dev/ai-lib#128 needs to merge, then re-pin `ai-lib` to it. The submodule currently points at an earlier commit on that PR's branch.

Known gap: Databricks OAuth sign-in isn't available in Assistant's provider screen on Positron yet, so its e2e test is skipped. Databricks personal access tokens and `.databrickscfg` work.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- AI provider sign-in now lives in Posit Assistant. Existing API keys and the Posit AI Pass sign-in carry over automatically.

### Validation Steps

The e2e suites below fail until the bundled Assistant is bumped (see above). _remove the `-` from the tag when ready for the tests to run_

- @:-assistant
- @:-workbench: Workbench sign-in for Anthropic, OpenAI and Posit AI
- @:-workbench-azure: Foundry shows as managed by Posit Workbench
- @:-remote-ssh: Assistant over remote SSH
- @:-web and @:-win: the Posit Assistant and notebook Assistant tests in the browser and on Windows

title: Add Data Explorer Refresh for Data Connections tables, keeping sort and filters
description:
## Summary

Tables opened in the Data Explorer from the Data Connections pane never showed changes made to the table outside Positron. Each driver built its view once, when the table opened, and cached the schema and row counts (SQLite also reads through a snapshot copied at open), so new or deleted rows stayed invisible until the tab was closed and reopened, which also lost the user's sort and filters. This PR adds a **Refresh** action for those tables. It rebuilds the driver's view from the table's current contents and reloads the grid and summary panel, keeping the user's sort and filters. Console data frames and DuckDB data files are unchanged; they already update on their own.

## Changes

**Refresh action**

- Refresh is the leftmost button in the right group of the Data Explorer toolbar, matching where refresh sits in the Data Connections and Variables panes. It is also in the Command Palette as "Data Explorer: Refresh".
- It is shown only when the table's provider supports refresh (SQLite, PostgreSQL, Redshift, Snowflake, Databricks, ODBC), and disabled while a refresh is in progress. Two new context keys drive this: `positronDataExplorerSupportsRefresh` and `positronDataExplorerIsRefreshing`.
- If the refresh fails (the table was dropped, or the connection is down), the existing data stays on screen and an error notification explains why. Clicking Refresh again while a refresh is running joins the one in progress.

**API and plumbing**

- New optional `refreshDataset?(datasetId): Thenable<void>` on `positron.DataExplorerRpcHandler`. It rebuilds the dataset's view, rejects on failure, and must leave the existing view intact when it does.
- The ext host reports whether a provider supports refresh when its handler registers (`$registerRpcHandler(providerId, supportsRefresh)`), and adds `$refreshDataset`. `MainThreadDataExplorer` tracks refreshable providers. `IDataExplorerRpcTransport` gains `supportsRefresh` and `refreshDataset`, and the service router delegates both to the owning extension host without activating a dormant provider.
- `PositronDataExplorerExtensionBackend`, `DataExplorerClientInstance`, and `PositronDataExplorerInstance` expose `supportsRefresh` and `refresh()`.

**Keeping sort and filters (`DataExplorerClientInstance.refresh`)**

- Sort keys and row filters are captured before the rebuild, then re-applied to the rebuilt view, matching columns by name, as the Python and R backends do when a data frame changes. A sort on a column that's gone is dropped. A filter on a column that's gone stays in the filter bar, marked invalid with "Column was removed", and isn't applied.
- The reload goes through the existing schema-update path, after waiting out any state request sent before the rebuild, so the grid never reloads from the old view's state.

**Drivers (SQLite, PostgreSQL, Redshift, Snowflake, Databricks, ODBC)**

- Each handler remembers how it built each dataset's view and implements `refreshDataset` by building the view again. The new view replaces the old one only after it has read its row count and has columns. A generation check stops a refresh that's overtaken by the dataset closing, reopening, or refreshing again from installing its view. SQLite drops the replaced view's snapshot.
- `setRowFilters` now checks filters itself, as Python's backend does, because the filter bar doesn't send back the validity a backend reported. A filter on a column the view doesn't have is reported invalid and not applied. If the combined filter fails, each filter is checked on its own with a scan-free query (`WHERE 1 = 0 AND (...)`), the ones that fail are marked invalid with the database's error, and the rest still apply.
- `setRowFilters` is now atomic: filters are committed only after their row count succeeds, so a filter the database can't evaluate no longer leaves the view unreadable. When requests overlap, the newest request that succeeds wins.

**Related fixes**

- `TableDataCache`: when a queued update was replaced by a later one (for example, a scroll queued behind a schema update), the replaced update's invalidation was dropped and stale cells could stay on screen. The invalidation flags are now merged.
- `TableDataDataGridInstance.setRowFilters`: when the backend rejects a filter change, the row filter bar re-reads the filters actually in effect and an error notification explains why. Before, the bar kept showing filters that weren't applied.

**Tests**

- Vitest: the client refresh (sort and filter remapping, invalid filters, fallback when filters can't be applied, rejecting without touching state, waiting out an earlier state request), the instance (joining a refresh in progress, error notification), the extension backend, multi-host routing of refresh, the `TableDataCache` merge, and the filter bar resync.
- Extension host: each driver's handler tests cover refresh (new row count, failed rebuild keeps the old view, close and reopen during refresh, SQLite snapshot cleanup, profile requests surviving a refresh on Redshift, Snowflake, and Databricks) and filter validation (the filter bar's round trip, a filter that can't be evaluated, failures no single filter causes, an unreachable source, overlapping requests). There's a new `sqliteDataExplorerRpcHandler.test.ts`, and one ODBC test now expects a regex filter to be marked invalid instead of rejected.

## Release Notes

#### New Features

- Tables opened in the Data Explorer from the Data Connections pane can now be refreshed to show changes made outside Positron. Sort and filters are kept. A filter whose column was removed stays in the filter bar, marked invalid. https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/issues/16717

#### Bug Fixes

- Fixed the Data Explorer filter bar showing filters that weren't applied after the backend rejected a filter change. It now shows the filters in effect and an error explaining why.

## Validation Steps

@:data-explorer @:connections

1. Open a SQLite database in the Data Connections pane and open a table in the Data Explorer. The Refresh button is the leftmost button in the right group of the toolbar.
2. Add rows to the table outside Positron (for example, with the `sqlite3` CLI) and click Refresh. The new rows and the new row count appear.
3. Sort by a column and add a row filter, change the table outside Positron, and click Refresh. The sort and filter are still applied.
4. Drop the filtered column outside Positron (for example, `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN`) and click Refresh. The filter stays in the filter bar, marked invalid with "Column was removed", and isn't applied. Add another filter: the grid still loads and the invalid filter stays invalid.
5. Drop the table outside Positron and click Refresh. An error notification appears, and the existing data stays on screen.
6. Open a console data frame or a CSV file in the Data Explorer. There is no Refresh button.

title: CI: add weekly npm audit and lockfile refresh for Positron-owned extensions
description:
Addresses posit-dev/positron-builds#1269

### Summary

This PR adds a weekly workflow that audits the runtime npm dependencies of the extensions that Positron owns. The workflow fixes the advisories that need only a lockfile refresh, and it opens one PR with the changes.

Snyk and Dependabot do not give us this signal:

- Both tools scan every manifest in the repository, which includes the upstream VS Code manifests. We get those bumps through upstream merges.
- Snyk does not open a PR for a transitive advisory when no direct upgrade removes it. A lockfile refresh fixes most of these advisories.
- Dependabot PRs get only Dependabot secrets and a read-only token, so our CI fails on them immediately (#16662). Also, the Dependabot rules that limit PRs to our paths live in the repository settings, not in the code. I decided to turn Dependabot alerts off after that trial, because I don't think it really helps us substantively.

The PR adds three files:

- `.github/dependency-audit-manifests.txt`: the 38 Positron-owned projects, one directory per line. When you add a new extension with its own `package-lock.json`, add it to this list. Maybe eventually we can add some automation to help us not forget this, but certainly it will be easier than the way Dependabot manages this in the GitHub UI.
- `scripts/dependency-audit.sh`: runs `npm audit --package-lock-only --omit=dev` on each project. With `--fix`, it first runs `npm audit fix --package-lock-only --omit=dev` in each project that has advisories. This stays inside the semver ranges in `package.json`. With `--snyk`, it also runs `snyk test`, so the report shows what the security team sees in Snyk. The script prints a Markdown report. You can also run it locally.
- `.github/workflows/dependency-audit-weekly.yml`: runs on Mondays and on `workflow_dispatch`, with a `dryrun` option. It uses the same managed-PR actions as the weekly test tag map check (`detect-managed-pr` and `commit-and-sync-pr`). The POSITRON_BOT app token opens the PR, so CI runs on it with the usual secrets. The report goes in the PR body and in the job summary.

The workflow stages only the lockfiles of the listed projects. It does not run `npm audit fix` in projects that have no advisories, because npm can rewrite their lockfiles with no real change.

On `main` today, the script finds runtime advisories in 5 projects. The fix clears 3 of them (Snowflake, `positron-ipywidgets/renderer`, and `positron-pdf-server`). It also removes the critical `proxy-addr` advisory in `positron-proxy`. The advisories that remain need a manual change:

- `positron-proxy`: 3 high, through `http-proxy-middleware`. The fix needs a semver-major bump.
- `positron-dev-containers`: 4 high, through `proxy-agent` and `basic-ftp`. No upstream fix is available.

Not in this PR: a check for deprecated packages (posit-dev/positron-builds#1270) and a Slack message. Dev dependencies are also out of scope for now.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- N/A

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

This PR changes only a scheduled workflow and a script that CI does not run on PRs. It needs no e2e tags.

1. Run the script locally from the repository root: `scripts/dependency-audit.sh`. Make sure that the report shows the 5 projects above.
2. Run `scripts/dependency-audit.sh --fix`. Make sure that only the lockfiles of those projects change. Then revert them with `git checkout -- extensions`.
3. After merge, start the workflow with `workflow_dispatch` and `dryrun: true`. Make sure that the Snyk column has numbers, not "error". I did not do a test of the Snyk step locally.

title: Add Positron commands for agents to look up help topics & vignettes
description:
Addresses #15724

> [!IMPORTANT]
> https://github.com/posit-dev/ark/pull/1438 needs to be merged. first. This PR bumps the ark submodule to that branch and relies on its updated help RPCs.

### Summary

Posit Assistant can call `positron.help.lookupHelpTopic`, but that only shows help to the user; the agent can't read it. This PR adds three agent-only commands that return locally installed R and Python documentation as Markdown, so the agent can answer questions about arguments, errors, and packages that are private, internal, or otherwise missing from its training data.

- `positron.help.readHelpTopic` reads a help page (signature, arguments, details, examples).
- `positron.help.listPackageDocs` lists a package's help topics and vignettes.
- `positron.help.readVignette` reads a vignette.

Each command takes an optional `languageId` and uses the foreground session if it matches, otherwise any running session for that language. Nothing is shown to the user.

**R:** backed by the `get_help_page`, `list_package_docs`, and `get_package_vignette` RPCs in Ark (posit-dev/ark#1438).

**Python:** the same three RPCs are added to the Python kernel. Help pages are rendered to Markdown from docstrings, with signatures and a list of public members for modules and classes. Topics are the package's public members, and the package README is exposed as its only vignette. PyPI distribution names (e.g. `scikit-learn`) resolve to their import names.

The `positron-commands` skill now tells the agent to read installed help before explaining how to use a function or package, its arguments, or an error it raises.

**Cleanup:** the old `vscode.lm` help tools in the R extension (`listPackageHelpTopics`, `listAvailableVignettes`, `getPackageVignette`, `getHelpPage`) are removed. They only existed to support the old Positron Assistant, which is gone, and nothing calls them anymore.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- Posit Assistant can now read help pages and vignettes from installed R and Python packages (#15724)

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:help @:assistant

Unit tests cover the new commands (`helpAgentCommands.vitest.ts`) and the Python RPCs (`test_help.py`).

1. Start an R session and ask Posit Assistant something like "What does the `.by` argument to `dplyr::mutate` do?" Verify it reads the help page (via `positron.help.readHelpTopic`) rather than guessing.
2. Ask "What vignettes does dplyr have? Summarize the colwise one." Verify it lists docs and reads the vignette.
3. Start a Python session and ask about `pandas.DataFrame.merge` arguments. Verify the help page comes back as Markdown.
4. Ask about a package by its PyPI name (e.g. `scikit-learn`) and verify it resolves.
5. Try a nonexistent topic or package and verify the agent gets a useful message back instead of an error.

title: Parse SQL in the editor with a WebAssembly analyzer, and use it for statement ranges
description:
Part of #16547; adds the statement ranges for #16545. **PR 2 of 4.** PR 1 (#16180) has merged, so this targets `main` directly. #16182 and #16183 are stacked on it.

### Summary

Teaches Positron to parse SQL. Adds the `sql-analyzer` Rust crate, compiled to WebAssembly and
committed, plus the `positron-sql` extension that loads it, and the first thing the parse is good
for: statement ranges.

Statement ranges are what Cmd+Enter uses to decide how much of the file to run. Until now a `.sql`
file had none, so there was no way to run the statement under the cursor. This is also the feature
the 2026.09 exploration (#15069) landed on as the right first one, because it applies to every SQL
dialect.

**Behind a flag.** Everything here waits for the `sql.enabled` setting (experimental, off by
default). With it off, the extension activates on a `.sql` file, reads the setting and stops: no
output channel, no providers, and the wasm is never read. Turning it on or off takes effect without
a reload.

**Why a wasm crate rather than a language server.** A language server is a process to launch,
supervise and tear down per workspace, and the editor features above this PR all need answers
during a keystroke. The analyzer is [`datafusion-sqlparser-rs`](https://github.com/apache/datafusion-sqlparser-rs)
behind a small op-based interface, compiled to wasm and called in-process -- no process lifecycle,
no IPC round trip, and the dialect coverage comes from a crate that already tracks it.

**What the analyzer answers.** Four ops, all per dialect:

- `statements`: statement extents. Used by this PR.
- `analyze`: syntax errors, and every table and column name a document refers to.
- `sources`: the tables, CTEs and aliases in scope at a cursor, with their columns where the SQL
  says them.
- `keywordsAt`: the cursor's position in the grammar (select list, FROM, after LIMIT, ...) and the
  keywords that belong there.

Only `statements` reaches the user here. The other three are what completion and diagnostics are
built on in PR 3, which brings the schema from data connections; they are tested here because this
is where they live.

**ggsql.** A statement can carry a ggsql plot after its query (`SELECT ... VISUALISE x, y DRAW
line`). The plot stays inside the statement's range, so Cmd+Enter sends both parts together, but
only the query in front of it is analyzed as SQL.

**The committed module.** The wasm is committed rather than built in CI, so a contributor without a
Rust toolchain can still build Positron. To keep it honest, `rust-toolchain.toml` pins rustc and
`wasm-fingerprint.txt` records a hash of the crate's inputs and of the module.
`Test: SQL Analyzer` (path-filtered to the crate) runs rustfmt, clippy and the crate's tests, and
fails if the inputs changed without a rebuild or the module changed without its inputs. It compares
fingerprints rather than rebuilding, because the same crate built with the same rustc gives
different bytes on macOS and Linux.

There is also a small core change: `vscode.executeStatementRangeProvider` threw when no provider had
a range, and now resolves to `undefined` (`extHostApiCommands.ts`).

### How to review

Most of the size is the crate: about half its lines are tests, and `resources/sql-analyzer.wasm`
is a 1.9 MB binary. The commits are each one change with a message saying why, so reading commit
by commit may be easier than reading the whole diff at once.

**Suggested order**

1. **`extensions/positron-sql/src/`** (about 600 lines of TypeScript). How the analyzer is used,
   before how it works. `extension.ts` loads the module and registers the one provider;
   `statementRange.ts` turns spans into a range, and `statementAt()` holds the "which statement
   does this cursor mean" rules; `analyzer.ts` is the wasm boundary (linear memory, JSON, and
   restarting the instance after a trap).
2. **`sql-analyzer/src/lib.rs`, then `api.rs`.** The crate doc explains the one-function JSON
   interface and why it is hand written rather than wasm-bindgen; `api.rs` has every request and
   response shape.
3. **`statements.rs`.** The only Rust module a user reaches through this PR. Edge cases worth a
   look: unterminated strings and comments, a final statement without a semicolon, and the
   VISUALISE split.
4. **The rest of the crate** (`cursor`, `keywords`, `scopes`, `sources`, `diagnostics`). These back
   completion and diagnostics, wired up in PR 3. Review them for structure and correctness rather
   than user-facing behavior.
5. **Build and CI.** `scripts/build-analyzer.mts` and `rust-toolchain.toml` (building the module
   and its fingerprint), `.github/workflows/test-sql-analyzer.yml`, and the small hooks in
   `build/filters.ts`, `build/gulpfile.extensions.ts`, `.vscode-test.js` and
   `scripts/test-integration*.sh`.

**Skimmable**

- `resources/sql-analyzer.wasm`: CI enforces that it matches the crate (see below).
- `tests/*.rs`: spot-check the scenarios rather than every assertion. `tests/generated.rs` builds
  statements by machine and checks completion positions against them, as a safety net.
- `keywords.rs` is mostly keyword lists, and `Cargo.lock` is generated.

**Where scrutiny is most welcome**

- **Trust in the committed binary.** CI proves nobody changed the crate without rebuilding the
  module, or the module without its crate. It does not prove the module was built from those
  sources, because the same build gives different bytes on macOS and Linux. Is that enough for a
  binary we ship, or should the module be built in CI or at release time?
- **`extHostApiCommands.ts`.** `vscode.executeStatementRangeProvider` now resolves to `undefined`
  instead of throwing when there is no range. Is there any caller that relied on the throw?
- **Trap recovery in `analyzer.ts`.** A Rust panic aborts and leaves the instance unusable, so the
  wrapper reports it and starts a fresh one. A failure should leave the user with "no range",
  never a broken analyzer.
- **Performance.** Every Cmd+Enter re-splits the whole document, uncached. Splitting tokenizes
  rather than parses, so it should be cheap, but it has not been measured on a very large file.

**Known limits, out of scope here**

- Runs in a Node extension host: Desktop, Server, Workbench, and remote hosts. There is no entry
  point for a browser-only extension host with no server.
- The dialect comes from the user's setting. Taking it from the active data connection arrives in
  PR 3.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- Experimental, behind the `sql.enabled` setting: Cmd+Enter runs the SQL statement under the cursor in a `.sql` file (#15069)

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:editor

No e2e tests are added. The parser's behavior is pinned where it lives: 168 tests in the Rust
crate, covering statement splitting, cursor positions, per-dialect keywords, scopes, diagnostics,
ggsql statements, and a generated set that checks completion positions over machine-built
statements. The `positron-sql` extension host suite (17 tests) covers the TypeScript side.

0. With `sql.enabled` at its default (off), open a `.sql` file and press Cmd+Enter: no statement
   range, and no "SQL" channel in the Output view. Then turn `sql.enabled` on; no reload is needed.
1. Open a `.sql` file containing several statements separated by semicolons.
2. Put the cursor in the middle of one and press Cmd+Enter. Confirm the highlighted range is that
   whole statement -- not the line, and not the file.
3. Confirm it works on a statement spanning several lines, and on one with a semicolon inside a
   string literal (`SELECT ';' FROM t;`), which must not split the statement.
4. Put the cursor at the end of `SELECT 1; -- note` and press Cmd+Enter: it runs `SELECT 1`. On a blank
   line between two statements it runs the next one; past the last statement, nothing runs.
5. Confirm an incomplete statement at the end of the file still gets a range rather than being
   dropped, and that comments after it are not part of it.
6. Confirm `SELECT * FROM t VISUALISE x, y DRAW point;` is a single range, ggsql part included.

title: Fix errors when MCP clients request screenshots
description: Fixes #16630 When an MCP client called `positronViewer.screenshot` through `run_positron_command`, the result was rejected by the 32 KB command result budget, so the agent got an error instead of an image. This PR makes the supervisor treat image results (`positron.ai.AgentCommandImage`) as images: - The command result budget no longer applies to image results. - The current plot is sent to Kallichore in the same image shape instead of a data URI, so `get_plot` and image-returning commands share one code path. Now the screenshot command works properly: Related PR: posit-dev/kallichore#83 turns image results into MCP image content blocks. The two must ship together; with the old Kallichore, `get_plot` would not recognize the new plot shape. > [!NOTE] > The Kallichore PR _must_ be merged first. I will coordinate merging both once they're approved. ### Release Notes #### New Features - N/A #### Bug Fixes - Viewer screenshots taken through the MCP server are returned as images instead of failing the size limit (#16630) ### Validation Steps @:mcp @:viewer @:plots 1. title: Add APIs for Posit Assistant to interact with Quarto notebooks
description: Part of #14733 ### Summary When a Quarto or R Markdown document uses inline output, its kernel runs as a notebook session, so Posit Assistant reaches for its notebook tools. Those tools only knew about the Positron Notebook Editor, so every call failed and the assistant had no way to run chunks or read their output. This PR lets the `positron.notebooks` API treat an open Quarto document with inline output as a notebook whose cells are its code chunks. Extensions can now read chunks, run them in the document's live kernel, read their inline outputs and execution state, add/edit/delete chunks (as text edits to the document, each undoable in one step), and clear outputs. Adding markdown cells and moving/reordering cells are rejected with a message pointing to the text tools, since that content lives in the document text. Fully addressing the issue also needs a change in Posit Assistant so it recognizes Quarto sessions and uses these tools; that will come in a separate PR in that repository. ### Release Notes #### New Features - Posit Assistant can run chunks and read inline output in Quarto documents that use inline output (#14733) #### Bug Fixes - N/A ### Validation Steps @:quarto @:positron-notebooks @:assistant New unit tests cover the Quarto notebook adapter, the chunk insert/replace edits, the output lookup, and the API routing. To test by hand (needs the matching Posit Assistant change): 1. Turn on inline output for Quarto (the `quarto.inlineOutput.enabled` setting). 2. Open a `report.qmd` with an R chunk such as `mean(mtcars$mpg)` and run it inline. 3. With the `.qmd` editor focused, ask the assistant to "Run the first chunk and tell me the result." 4. Check that the chunk runs in the document's kernel, the output appears inline, and the assistant reports the value. 5. Ask the assistant to add, edit, and delete a chunk; check that the document text updates and each change can be undone with one undo. 6. Ask the assistant to add a markdown cell or move a chunk; check that it gets a clear error and falls back to editing the text.

title: Add a Viewer stop button for extension preview panels (`PreviewPanel.stoppable`)
description: - Addresses #10753 - Related to https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto/pull/1193 ### Summary Extensions that show content with `positron.window.createPreviewPanel` can now show a stop button in the Viewer, with the first example being the Quarto extension. Before this PR, the Viewer had no stop button for a Quarto preview. This PR adds two members to `PreviewPanel`: - `stoppable`: the extension sets this to `true` while its process runs, and to `false` when the process stops. While it is `true`, the Viewer shows a toolbar with a stop button and a clear button. - `onDidRequestStop`: fires when the user clicks the stop button. The Viewer hides the button before it fires the event. The extension stops its process, and also decides if the preview closes. The Viewer does not try to find out if the process runs and instead, the extension owns that state. Panels from `previewUrl` keep their current stop button, which uses a `PreviewSource`. ### The approaches I tried before I had tried some other approaches for this, and WOW, they did not work out well. In one version, I gave `createPreviewPanel` panels a `PreviewSource`, the same as `previewUrl` panels. Positron found the terminal from the PID and watched it, showing the button while a process ran in the terminal, sending Ctrl+C on a click, and closing the preview when the process stopped. It did NOT work well and was QUITE a lot of code; having the extension in charge here turned out a lot better. ### Release Notes #### New Features - Extensions that use `positron.window.createPreviewPanel` can show a stop button in the Viewer with `PreviewPanel.stoppable` and `onDidRequestStop` (#10753) #### Bug Fixes - N/A ### Validation Steps @:viewer @:apps @:quarto Together with the Quarto PR at https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto/pull/1193: 1. Install the Quarto extension from the branch of the Quarto PR. 2. Open a `.qmd` file and run _Quarto: Preview_. 3. Make sure that the Viewer shows a stop button on the right side of its toolbar. 4. Save the document. Make sure that the button stays and that the toolbar does not move. 5. Click the stop button. Make sure that the preview server stops and that the preview closes. 6. Run _Quarto: Preview_ again. Press Ctrl+C in the Quarto Preview terminal. 7. Make sure that the stop button goes away and that the preview stays open. 8. Start a Shiny or Streamlit app with the App Launcher. Make sure that the URL bar and its stop button work as before.

title: Complete, lint and cross-reference SQL against the file's data connection
description:
Closes #15071, closes #15072, closes #16546. Part of #16547. **PR 3 of 4** -- stacked on #16181.

> Review this as the diff against `sclark/sql-2-analyzer`, not against `main`.

### Summary

Connects the parser from PR 2 to the schema from PR 1, so the editor can check SQL against the
database the user is actually connected to.

What a `.sql` file gets:

- **Table and column completions** from the connection's schema, scoped to the tables the statement
  actually reads from. The select after a `WITH` is offered the CTE's columns, not the columns of
  the tables the CTE reads from.
- **Diagnostics** for a name that does not resolve against the schema, with the aliases and CTEs a
  statement invents left alone -- `SELECT total AS t FROM orders ORDER BY t` is ordinary SQL.
- **Hover** showing a column's type and a table's shape.
- **Document links and references** from a name in the query to the row in the Data Connections
  pane, using the reveal command from PR 1.
- **Dialect-aware parsing and keywords**, resolved from the connection's driver. The map covers
  DuckDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redshift, Snowflake and Databricks plus BigQuery, MySQL and the
  per-database ODBC registrations, with a generic fallback for a driver it does not name.
- **A status bar item** naming the connection and dialect the file is written against, and letting
  the user change it.

**Scoping a file to one connection.** A `.sql` file is written against a particular database, so
each file is bound to one connection rather than completing against the union of everything open.
The binding is remembered per file, and a file with no connection gets keyword completions and the
generic dialect rather than a wall of errors.

On #15072: items 1, 2, 4 and 5 are here. Item 3 (progressive disclosure for large catalogs) is not
-- the schema is read in one bounded call per connection (depth 4, 200 per level, 5000 total)
rather than lazily. That is a deliberate mitigation, not lazy loading; lazy loading will be tracked
separately.

### Release Notes

#### New Features

- SQL files offer table and column completions from the connected database, and flag names that do
  not resolve against its schema (#15072)
- SQL completions and parsing follow the dialect of the connection's driver (#15071)

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:connections @:editor

No e2e tests are added; the editor features are covered by the `positron-sql` extension host suite
(232 tests), which is where the `vscode` API surface they are built on can actually be driven.

1. Connect to a PostgreSQL or DuckDB database with at least one table.
2. Open a new `.sql` file and confirm the status bar names the connection and its dialect.
3. Type `SELECT * FROM ` and confirm the connection's tables are offered.
4. Complete a table, add an alias, then type `alias.` and confirm only that table's columns appear.
5. Type a column name that does not exist and confirm it is flagged; rename it to a real one and
   confirm the diagnostic clears.
6. Write `SELECT total AS t FROM <table> ORDER BY t` and confirm `t` is **not** flagged.
7. Hover a table and a column and confirm the type and shape are shown.
8. Ctrl/Cmd-click a table name and confirm the Data Connections pane reveals that row.
9. Change the file's connection from the status bar and confirm completions follow it.
10. Open a `.sql` file with no connection and confirm keyword completions still work and nothing is
    flagged as unresolved.

title: feat: time out Data Connections look-ahead queries
description:
### Release Notes

A level in the Data Connections tree stays blank until every look-ahead metadata query for that level finishes. One slow or stuck query, common on cloud warehouses, holds back the other rows at that level, including rows that did not need a query of their own. If a query never returns, the level never appears. Before a level can render, each look-ahead awaits the group's children with no deadline. That wait covers both namespace groups and Views groups, so one hung fetch blocks every sibling. Nothing treats a fetch that simply never answers as a reason to keep the row and move on.

Each look-ahead now races its children fetch against a one-second timeout. If the timer wins, the look-ahead returns no children, the group stays as an ordinary row, and nothing is stored for a later expand. A response that arrives after the timeout is ignored, so it cannot be cached under a connection handle a reload has already dropped. Opening the row fetches the children again.

Closes #16657

- N/A

#### Bug Fixes

- N/A

Tests for the positron PathLookup change live in `src/vs/workbench/contrib/positronDataConnections/test/browser/dataConnectionsTreeInstance.vitest.ts`.

title: e2e: install Graphviz on Windows from the official zip, choco as fallback
description:
The Windows e2e Setup Graphviz step failed in [run 38935307640](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron/actions/runs/38935307640) because the Chocolatey community feed returned 504/504/503 on all three retries. Retrying choco can't get past a feed outage, so this PR adds a second source.

### Summary

Setup Graphviz now tries, in order:

1. **Cache.** A new `actions/cache` step keyed on the Graphviz version.
2. **Official zip** from the Graphviz GitLab package registry. It is checked against a pinned SHA256 (the same hash Graphviz publishes next to the zip). If the download or the check fails, the step deletes any partial extraction so a later attempt or the cache can't pick up a broken install.
3. **Chocolatey**, now pinned with `--version`.

Both sources are pinned to **16.1.0**. That is what choco has been installing on green runs, and it is the version the `graphviz-win32` master screenshot was rendered with. Without the pin, the two sources could install different versions and turn a feed outage into a screenshot diff. The version and hash are job-level env vars, and a comment says to bump them together with the screenshot.

The existing `nick-fields/retry` wrapper and the `dot -V` check stay, so a broken install still fails at this step and not later in the plot tests.

### Release Notes

#### New Features
- N/A

#### Bug Fixes
- N/A

### Validation Steps

@:win @:plots

I ran the step's script locally in pwsh 7 with `choco` stubbed out:

- **Rerun (cache hit):** skips the download (the stubbed `Invoke-WebRequest` would throw if called) and doesn't add the path to `GITHUB_PATH` twice.
- **Hash mismatch:** warns, removes the partial extraction, calls `choco install graphviz --version 16.1.0`, and continues.

In CI, the Windows lane should log `dot - graphviz version 16.1.0` from the zip path, and the Python static plot test should match its master screenshot.
